blocks.content: A pipe is the simplest and most familiar mechanism Unix provides for one process to send a stream of bytes directly to another. It is what makes a command like ls piped into grep work, and understanding exactly how it works under the hood connects directly back to the file descriptor mechanics from the file operations chapter.

This chapter covers anonymous pipes, the kind created with the pipe system call and used constantly by shells, named pipes for unrelated processes, and the blocking behavior that makes pipes act as a natural synchronization mechanism between a producer and a consumer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409297836-286997011.png
1. What a Pipe Actually Is

At its core, a pipe is a small, fixed size buffer maintained entirely inside the kernel, exposed to user programs as two file descriptors, one for writing into the buffer and one for reading out of it. Data written into the write end shows up, in the same order, at the read end, exactly like a real physical pipe carrying water in one direction.
This is strictly one directional. Bytes only ever flow from the write end toward the read end, never the reverse, a single pipe cannot be used to send data both ways at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409297836-389233743.png
2. Anonymous Pipes: Created With the pipe Call
blocks.text: 2. Anonymous Pipes: Created With the pipe Call

blocks.content: The pipe system call creates a new anonymous pipe and hands back two file descriptors in a single array: index 0 is the read end, and index 1 is the write end. This naming is easy to remember by thinking of it as matching standard input, descriptor 0, and standard output, descriptor 1, the read end behaves like an input, the write end like an output.

Because a pipe is anonymous, it has no name and no path anywhere on the file system, it exists purely as kernel state tied to these two file descriptors. This means only processes that already have one of these two descriptors, typically because they inherited it across a fork, tying directly back to the fork chapter, can actually use it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409297837-16738556.png
blocks.alt: Anonymous Pipes: Created With the pipe Call

blocks.title: A common convention worth internalizing
blocks.content: Whichever end a process does not intend to use is almost always closed immediately. A process that only writes closes its inherited read end, and a process that only reads closes its inherited write end, both to avoid confusion and because leaving a write end open anywhere prevents the reader from ever seeing a clean end of stream.

blocks.content: Every time a shell command like ls piped into grep runs, the shell is doing almost exactly what the code example above does. It creates a pipe, forks two children, one to run ls and one to run grep, and rewires each child standard input or output to point at the appropriate end of that pipe before calling exec.

blocks.content: The mechanism behind the wiring: dup2
blocks.text: The mechanism behind the wiring: dup2

blocks.content: The actual rewiring uses the dup2 system call, which makes one file descriptor number point at whatever an existing descriptor already points at. To make a command write into a pipe instead of the terminal, the shell calls dup2 to make file descriptor 1, standard output, point at the pipe write end, before calling exec on that command, tying directly back to the open file table entry mechanics from the file operations chapter.

blocks.content: 4. Blocking Behavior: A Built In Synchronization Mechanism
blocks.text: 4. Blocking Behavior: A Built In Synchronization Mechanism

blocks.content: A pipe kernel buffer has a limited, fixed capacity, it cannot grow without bound. This limited capacity gives pipes a genuinely useful side effect beyond just moving data: automatic flow control between a producer and a consumer, directly echoing the producer consumer problem from the synchronization module, just implemented for free by the kernel itself.

If a writer tries to write faster than a reader is consuming, and the pipe buffer fills up completely, the writer automatically blocks, pausing until the reader drains enough data to make room. Symmetrically, if a reader tries to read from an empty pipe with no data currently available, it blocks until the writer produces something.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409297837-380321661.png
blocks.alt: Blocking Behavior: A Built In Synchronization Mechanism

blocks.content: 5. Named Pipes, FIFOs: Pipes for Unrelated Processes
blocks.text: 5. Named Pipes, FIFOs: Pipes for Unrelated Processes

blocks.content: An anonymous pipe strictly requires a common ancestor, since the only way to actually get hold of its file descriptors is by inheriting them across a fork. This is a real limitation whenever two genuinely unrelated processes, with no shared ancestor at all, need to communicate this way.

A named pipe, also called a FIFO, first in first out, solves this by existing as an actual special file with a real path on the file system, created with the mkfifo command or call. Any process that can open that path, with no fork or shared ancestry required at all, can connect to it, one side opening it for reading, the other for writing, exactly the same underlying kernel buffer mechanism as an anonymous pipe underneath.

6. Two Way Communication Needs Two Pipes
blocks.text: 6. Two Way Communication Needs Two Pipes

blocks.content: Since a single pipe only ever flows in one direction, genuine two way communication between a parent and child, where both sides need to both send and receive, requires setting up two entirely separate pipes, one dedicated to each direction.

7. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming a single pipe can carry data in both directions, when it is strictly one directional, two way communication genuinely needs two separate pipes.","Forgetting to close the unused end of a pipe in each process, which can leave a reader waiting forever for an end of stream signal that never arrives because a stray write end is still technically open somewhere.","Trying to use an anonymous pipe between two processes with no common ancestor, when only a named pipe, FIFO, actually supports that."]
items: Assuming a single pipe can carry data in both directions, when it is strictly one directional, two way communication genuinely needs two separate pipes.

Forgetting to close the unused end of a pipe in each process, which can leave a reader waiting forever for an end of stream signal that never arrives because a stray write end is still technically open somewhere.
Trying to use an anonymous pipe between two processes with no common ancestor, when only a named pipe, FIFO, actually supports that.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain exactly why fds[0] is the read end and fds[1] is the write end, why pipes naturally block a writer on a full buffer and a reader on an empty one, and the specific limitation, requiring a common ancestor, that named pipes exist to solve.

Pipes are the simplest form of inter process communication, moving a raw stream of bytes with no structure of their own. The next chapter covers shared memory, a fundamentally different and much faster mechanism for processes to exchange data directly.
